newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban, foes gear up for new phase of Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: Taleban, foes gear up for new phase of Afghan war.

text.p: The purist Islamic Taleban and a northern alliance fighting it seem to be gearing up for the next potentially decisive phase of Afghanistan's 17-year war for power, Afghan watchers said on Sunday.
They said the Taleban had sent hundreds of fighters from Kandahar, where the militia is based, through the western city of Herat and up into the remote northwestern province of Bagdhis.

Their mission, said one Afghan source in contact with Herat, was to defend the 2,100-metre (6,890-ft) Sabzak pass, halfway between the city and the Bagdhis capital of Qalaye-i-Naw, against the forces of Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.
"I think the battle for Sabzak Kotal (pass) is going to be the next big one," the source said.
"If Dostum is clever, he'll put a lot of pressure there. It will at least distract the Taleban from the defence of Kabul and maybe even force them to weaken their lines," he said.
Fighting over a band of hills across the Shamali Valley 25 to 30 km (15 to 19 miles) north of the Afghan capital has been stalemated for two weeks.

Dostum and his ally, the ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani's military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, have battered at the Taleban defences with artillery, rockets, mortars, bombers and ground attacks, but have failed to make any significant impact.

Dostum has even sent warplanes to bomb Kabul, apparently aiming at the airport on the northeast edge of the city. He has failed to do any damage, apart from killing three children in a northwestern suburb.
"He may have achieved nothing substantial, but the raids are clearly keeping the Taleban on edge," said an Afghan watcher with a military background.
"It is possible that the battles north of Kabul are to keep the Talebnn occupied until winter comes, then the alliance can make its strike and Badghis could be a decisive element," he said."

The source said he saw no signs the largely ethnic Pashtun Taleban from the warmer south were preparing for winter battles around Kabul, where temperatures drop to minus 20 degrees Centigrade (minus 100 Fahrenheit) and snow falls thickly.
"The Taleban have fought well north of Kabul but they're fighting in sandals whereas Masood and Dostum's men are used to the cold and are equipped for it," he said.
"I think they'll wait to make their major move on Kabul until winter gets serious."
In the meantime, the war in Badghis could open up a major new threat to the Taleban if Dostum can take the Sabzak pass, the Afghan watchers said.
"If he takes Sabzak Kotal, then Herat is his," said the Afghan source. "If he has Herat, then Kandahar is threatened."
The two cities are at either end of the southern Afghan lowlands, where Dostum's tanks could be a major factor.
They said that it was not clear where the fighting was in Badghis, but the dispatch of significant Taleban reinforcements suggested it was of major importance.
The sources said a threat to Kandahar might make it difficult for the Taleban to maintain their lines north of Kabul because a significant proportion of their men were from the Kandahar region.
"The Pashtuns do not have a history of uniting for long and a threat to Kandahar could cause significant disharmony because some will want to leave (Kabul) and others won't," said one.

At the same time, Dostum, a former communist general who switched sides shortly before Moslem mujahideen toppled a Moscow-backed government in 1992 after 13 years of war, and Masood are known to dislike each other.
They were allied in 1992 and split bloodily two years later.
"They will probably hang together as long as there's a good chance of beating the Taleban. But even if they win, there's no guarantee they won't fight each other again," said one source.
